about: Fog of war from sensors (RK14, Atomic Rockets plan section 17): what a craft gives off, read from its power flow, and how far a contact could have gone since it was last seen.

eps.source: a typical radiator coating's emissivity, the value sse-light's radiators use

checks.says: heat to shed must be zero or more, got {}

references: Stefan-Boltzmann law: a surface of emissivity ε at temperature T sheds ε σ T⁴ per square metre (Rybicki, G. B. and Lightman, A. P. 1979, Radiative Processes in Astrophysics, Wiley, section 1.5). doi:10.1002/9783527618170

equation.name: How much radiator a craft needs to shed its heat
equation.formula: A = P / (eps * sigma * T * T * T * T)

P.name: heat the craft must shed at this temperature

eps.name: how well the radiator's surface glows (1 is a perfect black body)

source.text: Rybicki, G. B. and Lightman, A. P. 1979, Radiative Processes in Astrophysics

explain.curious: In space the only way to get rid of heat is to glow. Every watt a ship's reactor and engines waste must leave as infrared from its radiators, and that glow is what a telescope sees.
explain.science: Stefan-Boltzmann: the area of a grey emitter at T that radiates P.

gam.source: the heat capacity ratio of a monatomic gas or plasma, 5/3

checks.says: exhaust speed must be zero or more, got {}

references: Sutton, G. P. and Biblarz, O. 2017, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th edn, Wiley, chapter 3: an ideal nozzle turns the chamber's heat into exhaust speed, v² = 2 c_p T_c with c_p = γ k / ((γ − 1) m), so the chamber temperature behind an exhaust speed is T = (γ − 1) m v² / (2 γ k). https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Rocket+Propulsion+Elements%2C+9th+Edition-p-9781118753651

equation.name: How hot a drive's exhaust is, from how fast it leaves
equation.formula: T = (gam - 1) * mp * v * v / (2 * gam * k)

gam.name: heat capacity ratio of the exhaust gas

source.text: Sutton, G. P. and Biblarz, O. 2017, Rocket Propulsion Elements, 9th edn

explain.curious: Faster exhaust means hotter exhaust. A chemical rocket's flame glows white; a fusion torch's plasma is so hot it shines in X-rays and can be seen across a solar system.
explain.science: Ideal-nozzle energy balance: the chamber enthalpy c_p T becomes ½ v², with c_p = γ k/((γ−1) m).

share.source: stand-in share of the jet's power radiated by the plume (fudge register F56)

checks.says: jet power must be zero or more, got {}

references: SSE4 Atomic Rockets plan section 17 (accepted 23 Nov 2026): what a craft gives off comes from its power flow; a drive plume is seen by the light it radiates, a share of the jet's power. The share is a stand-in until plume spectra are modelled (fudge register). https://github.com/FrunkQ/star-system-explorer/blob/main/handover/design/SSE4-atomic-rockets-plan.md

equation.name: How much light a drive plume gives off

Pj.name: power carried away in the exhaust

share.name: share of the jet's power the plume radiates

explain.curious: A burning drive is the brightest thing about a ship. Even a small share of its power, given off as light, can be seen from far away.
explain.science: Plume luminosity as a fixed share of jet power; a stand-in for radiative cooling of the exhaust.

checks.says: speed must be zero or more, got {}
acceleration must be zero or more, got {}
time since last seen must be zero or more, got {}

references: Computed (SSE4, plan section 17.1): a contact last seen moving at v, able to accelerate at a, may be anywhere within v t + ½ a t² of where it was after t seconds; the textbook distance under constant acceleration (Halliday, D., Resnick, R. and Walker, J. 2013, Fundamentals of Physics, 10th edn, Wiley, chapter 2). https://www.wiley.com/en-us/Fundamentals+of+Physics%2C+10th+Edition-p-9781118230718
atoms.shown: r = v t + ½ a t²

equation.name: How far a contact could have gone since it was last seen
equation.formula: r = v * t + a * t * t / 2

v.name: speed it was last seen moving at

a.name: most its drive can accelerate it

t.name: time since it was last seen

r.name: radius of the ring it could be anywhere inside

source.text: Halliday, D., Resnick, R. and Walker, J. 2013, Fundamentals of Physics, 10th edn

explain.curious: Once you lose sight of a ship, all you know is where it was. The longer you wait, the bigger the circle it could be hiding in.
explain.science: Reach under constant acceleration from a known speed.
